INTRODUCTION

Imagine an unknown disease spreading across the United States, killing one person every thirty-four seconds and accounting for one out of every three deaths nationally. We would immediately classify it as a pandemic and shut everything down until we found a cure. Unfortunately for us, this disease already exists; fortunately for us, it is not contagious, although this may be the only fortunate part about it. Heart disease (or cardiovascular disease) is the leading cause of death among men and women in the U.S., and at times has accounted for over one hundred and sixty-eight billion dollars in healthcare spending in the span of only a year. For a disease as deadly and prevalent as heart disease, there is still much to be learned about it. Our group chose a data set documenting key features that can be used to predict heart disease to do some further investigation on its impacts. We specifically focused on potential prediction methods with the intention of finding a way to save as many lives as possible while also trying to cut down on the one hundred and sixty-eight billion dollars spent a year on services and medications. Through identifying possible interaction effects hidden in the clinical data set, we can build more efficient predictive models. This led us to focus our analysis on two specific diagnostic questions:

Question 1: Does the predictive power of ST in seniors persist after controlling for oldpeak?

Question 2: Does the effect of high fasting blood sugar on heart disease risk among patients with normal cholesterol levels differ by gender?

We first thought to ask, does the effect of high fasting blood sugar on heart disease risk among patients with normal cholesterol levels differ by gender? If this difference exists, how this interaction affects the predictive performance of the model. We will dive into the meaning and measurement of high fasting blood sugar in our data section, but this question essentially asks among patients categorized with normal cholesterol levels, how do blood sugar levels affect the risk of developing heart disease, and does gender change that impact? The difference in healthcare outcomes and treatments between genders has been well documented for a while, and a strong reason for the gap in treatment is due to the lack of research and data centered around women and women’s health issues. The difference in research quality on women’s healthcare compared to men’s is why we wanted to look at how the blood sugar level impacts change based on gender, and if there is any impact at all.

Our second question asked whether the predictive power of ST in seniors persists after controlling for oldpeak. We will dive deeper into the meaning of these variables in the data portion, but at its base level, oldpeak is the stress the heart experiences when exercising compared to resting, and ST is a type of electrocardiogram result, meaning the patient is experiencing ST-T wave abnormality. Finding a strong correlation between ST abnormalities and heart disease in seniors has the potential to cut down on the costs of diagnoses and increase accuracy, specifically in getting early diagnoses of patients during electrocardiograms, which is a big reason why we chose to focus on it in this follow-up. Getting accurate diagnoses quickly, especially when working with older populations, could be helpful in saving lives while also cutting down healthcare spending, and analyzing the electrocardiogram results among seniors could be the key to doing both.

With thorough analysis of the questions above we hope to discover relationships between common health markers and heart disease outcomes. Discovering any correlation could drastically decrease the leading cause of death among Americans while also saving potential billions of dollars used in healthcare spending on heart disease. Our findings could influence the way doctors go about diagnosing heart disease. Changing the way our nation’s worst killer operates may be closer than we think.

DATA

The dataset used in this analysis originates from a combined dataset of cardiovascular information across patients with and without cardiovascular disease. This data was found via Kaggle, but the data was originally collected by several international medical institutions across five datasets combined over eleven common features. Locations of data collection include the Hungarian Institute of Cardiology, the University Hospital in Zurich, the University Hospital in Basel, the V.A. Medical Center in Long Beach, and the Cleveland Clinic Foundation. The final, cleaned dataset consists of 918 unique observations, where each observation represents an individual patient’s clinical profile.

To answer our first question regarding the intersection of blood sugar, cholesterol, gender, and heart disease risk, we need to focus on four specific variables. The heart_disease variable is our target feature, which serves as a straightforward yes-or-no indicator of whether the given patient was diagnosed with heart disease. Alongside this is fasting_bs, which is another binary category indicating if the patient’s fasting blood sugar is high (greater than 120 mg/dl) or normal (less than 120 mg/dl). The patient’s sex is recorded with the sex variable. We use the cholesterol variable, which measures the amount of fats circulating in the blood, to filter our observations specifically to patients with normal cholesterol levels (under 240 mm/dl). After identifying the potential interaction effect, we extend our analysis by building predictive models. We use fasting blood sugar, gender, age, maximum heart rate, oldpeak, and exercise-induced angina as predictors. These variables are used to form predictive models in order to establish if using the model with this interaction improves our ability to predict heart disease.

For our second question about the predictive power of heart wave abnormalities in seniors after controlling for oldpeak, we need to analyze three additional variables. The age variable, measured in years, allows us to subset the data to senior patients (patients older than 60). We also examine resting_ecg, a categorical variable reflecting resting electrocardiogram results. You can think of an ECG as a map of the heart’s electrical system. We are specifically focusing on patients with ST wave abnormalities, which essentially means the heart’s electrical signals are showing signs of reduced blood flow or irregular rhythm. The other two ECG categories are normal (no abnormalities) and LVH, which indicates that the heart muscle might be overworked. Lastly, we use oldpeak. While it is technically a measurement of how much those electrical waves drop during a stress test, simply put, oldpeak captures how much the heart struggles or shows stress during exercise compared to when it is resting. We will use this variable to control for the severity of the overall ECG abnormality.

By isolating these specific metrics, we can thoroughly investigate the conditions that amplify cardiovascular risk. For our initial question, utilizing gender and blood sugar alongside our cholesterol filter allows us to explore hidden interaction effects that dictate a patient’s diagnosis and better build predictive models. For our second question, controlling for the severity of ST depression (oldpeak) will allow us to test the true predictive validity of resting ECG abnormalities in elderly patients. This variable selection ensures our predictive models are built on relevant, targeted clinical data rather than generalized noise.

RESULTS

RESULT 1

In answering our first research question – whether adding an interaction between fasting blood sugar and gender improves a model’s ability to predict heart disease among patients with normal cholesterol levels, beginning by examining how the effect of high fasting blood sugar on heart disease risk differs by gender.

In the data visualization, we see the percentage of patients with heart disease for different levels of fasting blood sugar levels by gender with cholesterol levels less than 240 mg/dl. According to the visualization, having high fasting blood sugar increases the rate of heart disease in both males and females. Nevertheless, there is a remarkable difference in how the rate is affected based on gender. For instance, the percentage of patients with heart disease among the female population increases drastically from 14% in those without high blood sugar to 75% in those with high blood sugar. The percentage for males, on the other hand, increases from 56% to 84%. Although both groups are at a higher risk, the level of change is much higher in the case of females. This pattern suggests that gender may influence how fasting blood sugar affects heart disease risk, motivating further statistical analysis.

To formally evaluate this observation, we fitted a logistic regression model using a train-test split including fasting blood sugar, gender, and an interaction term between the two variables. This regression allows us to estimate the effect of fasting blood sugar level on the risk of heart disease while allowing for a different impact based on sex. We have observed that the interaction term is statistically significant (p=0.0458). Moreover, the coefficient of interaction is negative, which means that the higher impact of risk due to increased fasting blood sugar is experienced by female patients more than by males.

In order to check how the interaction affects prediction modeling, various models were generated and then compared for performance. The following models were compared: the naive benchmark, the logistic regression without interaction, the logistic regression with interaction of fasting blood sugar and gender, the decision tree model, and XGBoost model. The naive baseline model does not use any predictors and simply assigns the majority class. The basic logistic regression model included fasting blood sugar, gender, age, maximum heart rate, oldpeak, and exercise-induced angina as predictors. The interaction logistic regression model used the same predictors but additionally included the interaction between fasting blood sugar and gender. The decision tree model and XGBoost model used the same set of predictors as the basic logistic regression model.

Model Performance Comparison
Accuracy and AUC on Test Data
Model Accuracy AUC
Naive Baseline 0.6486 NA
Logistic (Basic) 0.8108 0.9040
Logistic (Interaction) 0.8468 0.9247
Decision Tree 0.7928 0.8540

The accuracy of the naive benchmark is 0.6486 by predicting that all patients do not have heart disease, which shows the presence of class distribution but does not have any predictive value. On the other hand, all other models have shown improvement in terms of accuracy and AUC, which signifies better predictive capabilities. When comparing the logistic regression models, the logistic regression model with interaction is more accurate than the simple model. It has an accuracy of 0.8468, while the basic logistic model has an accuracy of 0.8108. The former model also has a higher AUC, which is 0.9247 compared to 0.9040 for the latter one. The decision tree model has a lower level of accuracy compared to the basic logistic model (0.7928), though a somewhat lower AUC (0.8540), implying that even though it is fairly successful, it does not quite explain the underlying relationship between the variables like the logistic model. XGBoost model shows the similar accuracy and AUC as desicion tree model.

In conclusion, the outcomes obtained from various analyses provide clear indications that gender acts as a moderator in the association between the fasting blood sugar level and the likelihood of developing heart disease. From the visualization, we note variations in the rates based on gender; from the logistic regression analysis, we have statistical evidence of the interaction effect. By building different models, we can see that the introduction of the interaction term enhances the accuracy of predictions and offers more insights into the relationship between fasting blood sugar and gender concerning heart disease risk.

RESULT 2

To investigate whether the predictive power of ST in seniors persists after controlling for oldpeak, we isolated a subset of patients over the age of 60. We first visualized the raw distribution of heart disease using a faceted bar chart, categorizing patients by their oldpeak levels and resting_ecg results. This initial exploration revealed that while heart disease rates generally increased with higher oldpeak values, the impact of the resting_ecg categories – Normal, ST, and LVH – appeared inconsistent across the different groups. Based on the visualized data, the independent predictive power of resting ST abnormalities is contingent upon the patient’s oldpeak level. While ST serves as a superior indicator of disease in the low and middle-aged oldpeak subgroups, its comparative advantage is lost in the high-risk subgroup. In this high oldpeak group, the severity of oldpeak acts as a saturating variable, resulting in a uniform 100% disease prevalence that renders resting_ecg classifications non-discriminatory.

In order to investigate the interaction effect between oldpeak and ST further, we employed a Logistic Regression framework to model the binary outcome of heart disease presence. Here, Normal and LVH were combined as the reference category; while these groups differ in baseline risk, as shown in the previous bar plot, this simplification is consistent with our research question targeting the independent contribution of ST specifically. The modeling process followed a hierarchical approach to identify the simplest effective fit. We evaluated three models: (1) a “Reduced” model focusing only on oldpeak, (2) an additive “Full Model” incorporating ST status, and (3) an “Interactive Model” to assess if the relationship between oldpeak and risk varied significantly across ST status. The first stage of analysis evaluated whether adding the ST improved the “Reduced” model containing only oldpeak. From the table, we see that the comparison between the model with oldpeak only and the additive model (oldpeak + ST) yielded a deviance reduction of 2.7078 on 1 degree of freedom. This resulted in a p-value of 0.0999. While oldpeak remains a highly significant individual predictor (\(p < 0.001\)), the inclusion of the ST categorical variable is only marginally significant at the \(\alpha = 0.10\) level and fails to meet the standard \(\alpha = 0.05\) threshold, suggesting that ST adds only limited additional information with only weak evidence that ST persists to predict the heart disease. Within the summary of additive model, the specific p-value for the ST variable (\(p = 0.110\)) further suggests that ST does not provide a statistically significant improvement in model fit over the effect of oldpeak alone.

The second stage of analysis tested the hypothesis that the relationship between oldpeak and heart disease risk varies depending on the patient’s ST status. We see from the table below that comparing the additive model (oldpeak + ST) to the interactive model (oldpeak * ST) yielded a deviance reduction of only 0.2626 with a p-value of 0.6084. The results indicate that there is no significant interaction between oldpeak and ST. The interaction term itself was highly non-significant (\(p = 0.616\)) in the summary table as well, suggesting that the slope of the risk increase associated with oldpeak is consistent and not depending on ST. Because the interactive model failed to explain significantly more variance than the simpler additive model, we fail to reject the null hypothesis of no interaction. Combined with our previous analysis, we see that ST does not provide additional predictive value once we already know the oldpeak value. We also see that both summary tables showed that oldpeak is the primary significant driver of risk within this dataset (\(p < 0.001\)).

In fact, to further visualize the model’s behavior, we generated an animated logistic curve using the full-model, showing the predicted probability of heart_disease as oldpeak increases. The animation illustrates a positive correlation: as oldpeak rises, the probability of disease climbs sharply. Interestingly, the curves for the different resting_ecg types are most distinct at lower levels of oldpeak but converge as oldpeak values exceed 3.0. This suggests a “ceiling effect” where even relatively high levels of oldpeak become such an overwhelming indicator of risk that the ST result becomes mathematically negligible in senior group. Once a senior reaches an oldpeak of 5 or 6, the ST result almost doesn’t matter anymore; the probability of heart disease is approaching 1.0 (100%) regardless. The clinical “signal” from the ST is drowned out by the severity of oldpeak. Recall our previous analysis. Looking at this plot, we can actually see why it wasn’t significant. While there is vertical separation, the slopes of the three lines are nearly identical, meaning that ST doesn’t change the fundamental relationship between oldpeak and heart disease. This suggests that while ST provides some baseline differentiation, oldpeak serves as a dominant and universal clinical indicator of heart disease risk regardless of the underlying ECG classification.

To further validate our statistical findings, we evaluated it using a ROC curve and confusion matrix with the Youden-optimal threshold. We compared the predictive performance of the reduced model containing only oldpeak against the full model that additionally incorporates ST. As shown in the ROC curves and comparison table below, the two models perform nearly identically across all evaluation metrics. Adding ST to the model increased AUC only marginally from 0.668 to 0.693, and Balanced Accuracy improved by less than 0.5 percentage points (0.668 to 0.672). These negligible gains in real-world predictive performance corroborate our earlier deviance analysis, which found that ST failed to meet the standard significance threshold of α = 0.05. Taken together, the statistical and predictive evidence converge on the same conclusion: ST abnormalities do not meaningfully enhance the model’s ability to classify heart disease beyond what oldpeak already captures. In the senior population, oldpeak stands as the dominant and sufficient predictor, and the additional clinical information carried by resting ECG ST classification contributes negligible practical value.

An unusual phenomenon observed in both the animation and the raw data was that the Normal ECG group showed a higher predicted risk than the LVH group. In many clinical datasets, LVH (Left Ventricular Hypertrophy) is considered a higher-risk marker than a Normal ECG. However, our plot shows the “Normal” group consistently has a higher predicted probability than the “LVH” group. While clinically counter-intuitive, this likely stems from a disparity in sample sizes within the senior subset, where a smaller number of LVH observations (only 59) may lead to higher variance and less stable coefficients in the model. This counterintuitive result may also reflect the influence of other dominant risk factors, potential survivor bias, or reduced discriminative power of LVH in older populations. Despite this discrepancy, the consistent slope across all three curves reinforces our statistical finding: while ST results shift the baseline risk slightly, they only offer a little bit of extra information and do not fundamentally alter the primary relationship between oldpeak and the likelihood of heart disease.

CONCLUSION

In this study, we set out to answer two main questions about predicting heart disease. First, we asked whether the effect of high fasting blood sugar on heart disease risk differs by gender among patients with normal cholesterol levels. Our results showed that gender does play an important role and the interaction between fasting blood sugar and gender significantly improved the model’s predictive ability. The logistic regression model with the interaction performed slightly better than the other models with higher accuracy and AUC than the others. Second, we asked whether ST abnormalities still help predict heart disease in seniors after controlling for oldpeak. We found that it provides very small improvements to prediction. Once oldpeak is included in the model, ST adds very little predictive value. An interesting takeaway that we found is how strong the gender difference was in the first question and how little impact ST had in the second.

Heart disease remains one of the leading causes of death and a major source of healthcare spending, making these findings very important. Being able to predict risks surrounding heart disease better can help doctors make faster and more accurate decisions. From our first question, the results suggest that high fasting blood sugar should not be treated the same for all patients. Female patients appear to experience a larger increase in risk, which means doctors may need to take a more targeted approach when evaluating patients. From our second question, the results show that oldpeak is a much stronger and more reliable indicator than ST abnormalities in seniors. This can help simplify the diagnostic process by putting more focus on the most important variables instead of relying on measures that add little value. Overall, these results support the idea that data-driven models can improve how heart disease is identified and managed, which can lead to better outcomes and potentially lower costs.

Several limitations in this analysis should be considered. First of all, the dataset contains only 918 patients and was combined from multiple hospitals. This may introduce inconsistencies in how the data was collected. The dataset also does not include important lifestyle factors such as diet, exercise, or smoking, which could have a strong impact on heart disease risk. Some groups in the data were also smaller than others, which may have affected the stability of certain results. From a modeling perspective, we focused mainly on logistic regression and decision trees. While these models performed well, more advanced methods such as random forests or boosting techniques could potentially improve prediction accuracy. Research in the future could use larger and more diverse datasets, include additional variables, and explore more complex models to better understand the factors that drive heart disease risk.
